Photograph: Murad Sezer/Reuters View image in fullscreen The burned-out Russian-flagged cargo ship Omskiy-107 lies beached off the Turkish coast near Istanbul. Photograph: Murad Sezer/Reuters Ukraine Deadly escalation in Black Sea attacks prompts fears of even higher food prices Russian and Ukrainian strikes in July killed more crew than in whole war to that month, preventing grain exports Joanna Partridge Fri 4 Sep 2026 10.35 EDT Last modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A summer of hostilities in the Black Sea proved deadly for seafarers, as Russia and Ukraine attacked each other’s ships and port infrastructure, preventing vital grain exports and prompting concerns that the conflict will push global food prices even higher. More crew were killed in the Black Sea in July than during the entirety of the war before that month as the conflict has intensified , making the body of water the most dangerous in the world for commercial shipping. This is despite the conflict between the US and Iran, with vessels still being targeted in the strait of Hormuz , Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. As many as 23 people died in July as a result of attacks on 35 ships in the Black Sea, according to estimates from the Turkish seafarers’ union Türkiye Denizciler Sendikası. Attacks on vessels continued into August and escalation in the Ukraine war has prompted the head of the UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization, to condemn the “deterioration of maritime security around the globe”. Russia first launched waves of attacks on port infrastructure and vessels anchored in Ukrainian Black Sea ports in the months after its invasion in 2022, preventing Kyiv from exporting grain . In July, Russia again struck Ukraine’s main grain export hubs of Odesa and Chornomorsk. View image in fullscreen Firefighters tackle a blaze on a civilian vessel hit during Russian missile strikes on Chornomorsk last December. Photograph: State Emergency Service Of Ukraine/Reuters However, the recent escalation in the Black Sea and neighbouring Sea of Azov – connected by the Kerch strait – has also resulted from Ukrainian retaliatory attacks. Drones have hit Russian vessels, including tankers Kyiv says belong to a shadow fleet of hundreds of ships used by Russia to evade sanctions on its oil exports. Ukraine has targeted ships and port buildings at the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, vital for oil and grain exports. In a grim illustration of the danger to vessels and their crew, an abandoned Russian-flagged cargo ship – with a burned-out command deck – recently ran aground on Turkey’s Black Sea coast as startled holidaymakers looked on. The Omskiy-107’s crew abandoned ship after it was hit by a Ukrainian drone near Novorossiysk, leaving the unmanned vessel to drift hundreds of miles and end up close to the Bosphorus, the narrow strait straddled by Istanbul that is one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes. View image in fullscreen A damaged Liberian-flagged bulk carrier is escorted by a safety boat through the Bosphorus this week. Photograph: Murad Sezer/Reuters Shipping in the region is under increased threat, according to analysts at the maritime risk intelligence firm Vanguard. “Merchant vessels are now more likely to be affected because of the ports they visit, their trading activity and the cargoes they carry. Attacks have also extended beyond ports and their immediate approaches, increasing the risk to vessels across a wider area of the Black Sea,” they said. The precarious maritime situation has already significantly reduced Russian and Ukrainian grain exports, raising concerns the disruption will worsen the impact of other food price shocks and hurt countries reliant on imported wheat, barley and maize. Russia is the world’s largest grain exporter, with its produce mostly going to the Middle East and north Africa, particularly Turkey and Egypt, while Ukraine is the fifth-largest. In July, Russia suspended shipping in the Sea of Azov after a wave of Ukrainian drone attacks, before deciding to redirect some grain exports to alternative routes such as via the Caspian and Baltic seas and the Pacific. However, more than 70% of Russia’s seaborne grain exports are shipped from Black Sea ports, and a further 20% from the Sea of Azov, according to analysis from Oxford Economics. “I have seen estimates that Russian grain exports were down to 40% of normal export capacity in August,” said Tatiana Orlova, the lead emerging markets economist at Oxford Economics. View image in fullscreen A satellite image shows damage to a grain conveyor, after a Ukrainian drone and missile attack on Novorossiysk last month. Photograph: Vantor/Reuters Ukraine, which had a bumper and early grain harvest this year, has also found itself unable to export large volumes through its Black Sea ports. Kyiv exported only a third – about 1.4m tonnes – of the grain it could have exported, using sea, rail, river and road, according to recent comments from Ukraine’s food minister. Global wheat prices have been trading higher in recent weeks, but remain below levels at the beginning of the Ukraine war in 2022. However, analysts say the latest disruption to seaborne grain exports is likely to push prices higher and exacerbate other food supply shocks, including the Iran war and lower European grain yields after extreme summer heat and the rapidly developing El Niño weather system . Global food prices are forecast by Oxford Economics to rise by nearly 12% this year and a further 4.8% in 2027. Unlike in 2022, when many big food importing countries were caught napping by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, “a lot of countries have grain stocks, which should help, so there is better preparedness for this kind of shock”, said Orlova. “But it is pretty clear the food price is going to be affected.” Explore more on these topics Ukraine Russia Shipping industry Water transport International trade Turkey Global economy news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Russia strikes Ukraine intelligence HQ in ‘major escalation’ Grinding up fish to feed to fish is ‘absurd’: fears over UN aquaculture plan Bhutan hosts first ‘conscious food summit’ amid threats to global supplies Europe calls out Russia’s ‘hybrid war’ in public. Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/AAP View image in fullscreen Victoria’s deputy premier, Gabrielle Williams (centre), will announce a rollout of new portable ultrasound machines, which will make it easier for women to access medical abortion. Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/AAP Victorian politics Victorian Labor puts reproductive rights on election agenda as it warns One Nation could try to wind back abortion access Exclusive: ‘We don’t want to see any winding back of women’s rights,’ health minister says ahead of state election Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Benita Kolovos Victorian state correspondent Wed 23 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 11.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Victorian Labor government is announcing new measures to improve access to medical abortion, as it puts reproductive rights on the election agenda and claims One Nation could use abortion as a negotiating chip with the Coalition in the event of a hung parliament. On Thursday, the deputy premier and minister for women, Gabrielle Williams, and the health minister, Ingrid Stitt, will announce a rollout of new portable ultrasound machines for the state’s 20 sexual and reproductive health hubs. The machines, costing $480,000, will help confirm early pregnancy sooner, making it easier for women, particularly in regional Victoria , to access medical abortion – a drug-induced termination that can be carried out up to nine weeks’ gestation. One Nation’s lurking attachment to the fringe anti-abortion movement sounds like the start of a horror movie | Van Badham Read more “It means women, particularly in regional Victoria, will be more likely to be scanned within that nine-week window for medical abortion, rather than having to wait or travel long distances to get a scan, and by then potentially only have surgical abortion options available for them,” Stitt said. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Abortion was decriminalised in Victoria in 2008, with women able to obtain a termination during the first 24 weeks of pregnancy, and later if they obtain the agreement of two doctors. Stitt said since then Labor had been working to make public abortion care safer – via the introduction of safe access zones around clinics in 2015 – and more accessible, including through the mobile women’s health clinic and virtual women’s health clinic . The latter reported nearly 60% of its appointments in its first year supported medical abortion. “We don’t want to see any winding back of women’s rights to choose or their access to safe care across the state,” Stitt said. “We’re proud of the investments that we’ve made, and we will be fighting hard to protect them in the election campaign.” Earlier this month, the Victorian opposition leader, Jess Wilson, emphatically ruled out any changes to the state’s abortion laws under a Coalition government. It followed the release of a video by a market research company linked to Labor, which claimed that Wilson had “handpicked Liberal candidates who want abortion banned” and stated that One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, wanted to make abortion a crime. View image in fullscreen Warren Pickering. The One Nation Victoria leader said in 2024 that the state’s abortion laws were ‘some of the most draconian on the planet’. Photograph: James Ross/AAP “Victorians can’t risk a Liberal One Nation government and the polls show the Liberals can’t govern without One Nation,” the video said. Wilson told the Age: “Abortion law will not change under a Liberal and Nationals government. Full stop.” She repeated the comments in a video with the Herald Sun at the weekend. But the deputy premier said Wilson “might not be the one calling the shots”, given current polling suggested the Coalition was short of an outright majority. “With the way the polling is lining up, this is potentially a situation where One Nation aren’t a minor partner – they’re potentially an equal partner – so her ability to push back on that might be restricted,” Williams said. One Nation’s national platform pledges to “seek every opportunity to roll back brutal and extreme abortion law”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion The federal leader, Pauline Hanson, has said she was not against abortion in the first trimester , a position that has not been reflected in the party’s formal policy. ‘Made a mistake’: One Nation’s NSW leader says party wants to restrict abortions, not stop them Read more Last week, its New South Wales leader Mark Newman attended a rally alongside the controversial campaigner Joanna Howe, which was calling for the NSW parliament to restrict abortion access. At the rally he said One Nation “want to stop” abortion and that if elected, would ensure there was a “right to life … that babies live”. He later said One Nation does not advocate for an outright ban on abortion and had been speaking about late-term abortions and terminations for sex selection. Barnaby Joyce appeared at a June event that was organised by Howe, who also campaigned in the lead-up to the Queensland and South Australian state elections. In 2024, Pickering joined pro-life activists at a “March for Babies” in Melbourne and posted on Facebook that Victoria’s abortion laws were “some of the most draconian on the planet”. Williams said: “It’s not unreasonable to be asking at what point the Liberal National Coalition are prepared to walk away from One Nation if this is the position they are taking to the election – as their counterparts have in other states.” The deputy premier denied Labor was conducting a scare campaign. “This is a genuine question being asked on the back of positions that are being expressed by One Nation around the country,” she said. “Where’s the line?” Pickering has been approached for comment. Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen A police officer stands guard outside the church where a shooting attack occurred during a funeral in Karak, Jordan, on 23 October. Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock Jordan Seven killed and 40 injured after gunmen open fire at church funeral in Jordan Footage broadcast on state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots Associated Press Fri 23 Oct 2026 21.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others, authorities said. The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 180km (110 miles) south of the capital, Amman. Footage broadcast on Jordanian state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots. A third man who appears to be holding a semiautomatic rifle then approaches and opens fire, and all three then run toward the church. Video footage taken by witnesses shows broken glass and pools of blood on the floor of the church. Dorgham Halasa, who was among the mourners inside the church, said intense gunfire erupted 15 minutes after the funeral had started, and then people started running. “It was a weird situation, and heavy gunfire,” Halasa said. He did not see the gunmen, but said other people reported seeing four of them. The Associated Press could not independently verify the number of assailants, and Jordan’s security services did not immediately release details. A government statement said that the attack was “carried out by unknown assailants,” but didn’t say whether any gunmen were captured or killed. It said that “investigations are under way at full speed”. Jordan declared three days of national mourning, according to the kingdom’s Petra news agency. Karak is home to a minority Christian population. In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed those gunmen after a long standoff. Jordan’s health minister Ibrahim al-Budour said two of those wounded are in critical condition. King Abdullah II said on X that Jordan “will confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties” and offered his “deepest condolences to the families of the martyrs, and our wishes for recovery to the wounded”. Jordan’s prime minister Jafar Hassan said during a security meeting in Karak on Friday evening that the attack was a result of terrorist ideology and blind extremism. He said the assailants will be punished and legal measures taken against those who seek to introduce extremism. Condemnation of the slayings came from around the region, including from Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Oman. Ahmed al-Tayeb in Cairo, the grand imam of Al-Azhar, the Sunni Muslim world’s foremost religious institution, offered his condolences to the families of victims in Friday’s shooting, calling it a “heinous terrorist attack.” Iraqi foreign minister Fuad Hussein called his Jordanian counterpart and “affirmed Iraq’s solidarity with Jordan in the face of terrorism”, Hussein’s office said in a statement. UN Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the attack during a funeral as “especially heinous,” spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said. “The secretary-general also calls for all those responsible to be found and to be held to account.” Explore more on these topics Jordan Middle East and north Africa Christianity news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
